new_statements.quote: The foot is a rhythm unit bounded by slight decreases in tempo and including one stressed syllable. Stressed syllables have greater intensity or greater duration, or both, than unstressed syllables of comparable segmental composition. The placement of stress within a foot is predictable on the basis of the distribution of long and high syllables (defined at the end of 3.) in that foot. If a foot contains a long syllable (and no foot contains more than one long syllable), that syllable is stressed. Otherwise, the first high syllable of the foot is stressed. In feet with only short low syllables, the penultimate syllable is stressed. The only syllable in a monosyllabic foot is stressed by definition.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is fully predictable within the foot (a rhythm unit of 1-4 syllables). A long syllable (one containing two or more vowels: a long vowel or a diphthong, e.g. foo 'bird', bakaa 'white man', baaka 'black'; at most one per foot) takes the stress. If there is no long syllable, the first syllable bearing a high tone is stressed. If all syllables are short and low-toned, the penult is stressed (e.g. sabaku 'wading bird'). A monosyllabic foot is stressed by definition. The authors explicitly choose a two-tone-plus-sandhi analysis over a pitch accent one because it makes stress predictable (p. 6: 'given a system of two tones with tone sandhi rules, stress can be predicted as described below'); tone, not stress, is the contrastive suprasegmental.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No notion of secondary stress. A stem carrying more than one stressed syllable is analysed as spanning more than one foot (p. 6: 'If more than one syllable is stressed, the stem forms part of more than one foot'); e.g. kaa/basi 'gourd' = two feet (fn. 9).
new_statements.exceptions: (a) When tone sandhi changes which syllables are high in a surface form and the stem has no long syllable, stress placement 'varies freely' between the underlying-form position, the first (or every) surface high syllable, or the penult, or all syllables get comparable duration/intensity: tabiki 'island' [ta'biki ~ 'tabiki ~ tabi'ki ~ tabiki] (pp. 6-7). (b) Long syllables always keep their stress in surface forms: wooko ['wooko], never *[woo'ko] (p. 7). (c) For the stress rule 'long' means two or more vowels only; a syllable closed by /N/ is merely phonetically longer than an open one and is not counted as long (p. 5). (d) Epenthetic vowels after /s/ (sitali 'star') and syllabic /N/ are always low-toned and unstressed (pp. 2-4).
new_statements.identity_note: Huttar & Huttar 1972 describes Djuka (= Aukan / Ndyuka, ndyu1242) from fieldwork in Paramaribo, Dec 1968 - Mar 1969; the two principal informants were from Agitiondre on the Cottica River, others from Tottiekamp (lower Saramacca River) and Sara Kreek (near the Tapanahonij). The paper treats Paramaccan and Boni (Aluku) as separate polities with languages 'even more similar to Djuka than is Sranan' (fn. 1); it does not describe those varieties. The description is tentative for tone sandhi (p. 7) but the stress rule is stated without hedging.

tone_statements.citation: Yakpo, Kofi. 2021. Creole Prosodic Systems Are Areal, Not Simple. Frontiers in Psychology 12: 690593. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2021.690593
tone_statements.quote: The related Surinamese Maroon creole Ndyuka also has a two-way height contrast including tonal minimal pairs, e.g., tàkì /L-L/ ‘quotative complementizer’ vs. tákì /H-L/ ‘say’ (Huttar and Huttar, 1994, 5). Compounds are created via the same tonal derivation as in the African English-lexifier creoles, i.e., káw /H/ ‘chew’ and bón /H/ ‘bone’ → kàw-bón /L-H/ ‘chewed-bone(s)’ (Huttar and Huttar, 1994, 373).

sources.citation: Barth, Emily. 2016. Tone loss in Sranan Creole: re-thinking contact driven change. Papers in Historical Phonology 1: 76-89. doi:10.2218/pihph.1.2016.1694
sources.quote: Among the Surinamese creoles, Sranan is a stress-accent language whereas both Ndyuka and Saramaccan exhibit phonological tone in addition to stress.
sources.note: 'Among the Surinamese creoles, Sranan is a stress-accent language whereas both Ndyuka and Saramaccan exhibit phonological tone in addition to stress'; argues that liquid-cluster epenthesis and intervocalic liquid deletion (heavy syllables) in the maroon creoles contributed to the survival of distinctive tone, against the view that Sranan lost tone through Dutch-modelled complex onsets.
